newsitem.title: MALAWI: Fledgling Malawi debt mkt hampered by bureaucracy.
newsitem.headline: Fledgling Malawi debt mkt hampered by bureaucracy.

text.p: Stringent financial regulations and government bureaucracy were hampering the massive growth potential of Malawi's fledgling capital market, a leading stockbroker said on Thursday.

Stockbrokers Malawi Limited (SML) chief executive Rob Stangroom said high reserve ratios, strict rules on public borrowing as well as legislative anomalies made it difficult for institutions to trade in the market.
The Malawi money market currently has 660 million kwacha ($44 million) in long-term stocks and 2.2 billion kwacha ($146. million) in Treasury bills outstanding.

"It has tremendous potential to make progress but is hindered by high liquidity reserve ratios the Reserve Bank of Malawi imposes on qualifying financial institutions," Stangroom told Reuters in an interview.

Financial institutions are required to place 35 percent of their deposits with the central bank. Because the money market is so illiquid, investment opportunities are limited and institutions tend to hold on to their stock, he said.
And while Malawi companies were allowed to borrow from the general public, they have to do so under strict guidelines.
"At the moment, the private sector has no way to borrow directly from the public," Stangroom said.
Capital market development laws require that the Reserve Bank of Malawi decide on all capital market issues. But anomalies in the legislation means reference has to be made to the finance ministry.
"Government may not understand the private sector's need to develop this market but they are the ultimate decision makers," he said.
Stangroom also noted that SML had applied in February this year to launch commercial discount notes (CDNs) on the money market, but government has not yet approved the proposal.
"We are still waiting for government approval of the system," Stangroom said.
Once approved, the system would be managed by SML with assistance from Edwards and Company of Zimbabwe. He added that CDNs were expected to begin trading on the Malawi money market in 1998.
